before.zh: 魏元會，緭戲為詩曰：「帽上著籠冠，緭上著朱衣，不知是今是，不知非昔非。」

translations.literal: At the Wei New Year's assembly, Wei jestingly composed a poem saying: "On the hat one wears a caged crown, on Chi one wears vermilion robes; I know not whether now is now, I know not whether not-the-past is not-the-past."
translations.idiomatic: At the Wei court New Year's gathering, Wei penned a mocking verse: "A caged crown atop the hat, vermilion robes on Chi—who knows if this is now or then, if past and present aren't the same?"

after.zh: 魏元會，緭戲為詩曰：「帽上著籠冠，袴上著朱衣，不知是今是，不知非昔非。」

translations.literal: At the Wei New Year's assembly, Wei jestingly composed a poem saying: "Over the hat one wears a gauze cap, over the trousers one wears a vermilion robe; I do not know whether what is now deemed right is right, I do not know whether what was formerly deemed wrong was wrong."
translations.idiomatic: At the Wei court New Year's gathering, Wei penned a mocking verse: "A gauze cap over the hat, a vermilion robe over the trousers; who knows whether what is praised today is right, or what was condemned of old was wrong?"
translations.footnote: The digital base has 緭 in the verse's second line; the Nanjian and Jiguguge editions of Nanshi 61 and the inspected Liangshu 20 witness read 袴, 'trousers,' adopted here. The preceding 緭 names the poet, Wei. 籠冠 is a gauze cap; 是 and 非 play on judgments of right and wrong, not merely past and present.

evidence: G1: Hong Kong Education Bureau clothing resource, PDF page 93
decisions.reason: Independently inspected the Nanjian page 109, Harvard Jiguguge sequence 954 and Liangshu 20 page 77 scans: each has the clothing graph 袴 in the verse, while the preceding 緭 names its author. The replacement preserves the four-line garment/judgment contrast. 是/非 express approval and disapproval; the proposed right/wrong reading restores this wordplay without inventing an event. Gauze headgear is supported by the cited clothing reference. The footnote explicitly discloses the emendation.

before.zh: 榮乃為伐濟自硤石，與顥戰於河橋。

translations.literal: Rong then made rafts, crossed from Xiashi, and fought Hao at River Bridge.
translations.idiomatic: Rong then made rafts and crossed from Xiashi to fight Hao at River Bridge.

after.zh: 榮乃為伐濟自硤石，與顥戰於河橋。

translations.literal: Rong then made rafts, crossed from Xiashi, and fought Hao at River Bridge.
translations.idiomatic: Rong then made rafts and crossed from Xiashi to fight Hao at River Bridge.
translations.footnote: Nanshi 61's Nanjian edition reads 伐, retained here; its Jiguguge edition reads 栰, a variant of 筏, 'raft.' The inspected Liangshu 32 witness reads 縛木為筏, 'bound wood into rafts.' The translation follows the raft reading supported by these witnesses.

decisions.reason: Independently inspected Nanjian 伐, Harvard sequence 956 栰 and Liangshu 32 page 43 縛木為筏. The Ministry of Education variant dictionary confirms 栰 as a form of 筏. Keeping the attested base and approved raft English while explaining those precise witness differences is justified; the note does not claim 伐 and 筏 are generally interchangeable.

before.zh: 慶之在縣瓠，魏驍將堯雄子寶樂特為敢勇，求單騎校戰，昕躍馬直趣寶樂，雄即潰散。

translations.literal: When Qingzhi was at Xuanhu, Baoyue, son of Wei's fierce general Yao Xiong, was specially daring and brave; he requested single combat on horseback; Xin leaped on his horse and charged straight at Baoyue; Xiong immediately routed and scattered.
translations.idiomatic: At Xuanhu, Yao Xiong's son Baoyue, a Wei champion, challenged anyone to single combat. Xin spurred straight at him. Yao Xiong's force broke and fled.
